h: Welsh bluestones and a landscape full of secrets
p: The stones themselves are only part of the puzzle. The big sarsens came from the Marlborough Downs area, roughly 15 to 20 miles north, but the smaller bluestones were brought all the way from the Preseli Hills in west Wales, well over a hundred miles away. More recently, researchers found that the Altar Stone, lying at the heart of the circle, came from north-east Scotland. Just how these ancient people moved such massive stones over that distance is still a big part of the mystery.

From the visitor centre, a shuttle bus takes you to the stones, but walking across the open landscape is a lovely alternative if the weather is kind. Along the way you'll pass burial mounds and earthworks that are part of a much bigger prehistoric landscape, and it starts to sink in how important this whole area must once have been.

At the summer solstice, crowds gather to watch the sun rise over the stones, a tradition that now draws thousands of people. If you'd rather a calmer visit, aim for early or late in the day outside the main holidays.

Don't stop at Stonehenge. On the edge of Amesbury, Woodhenge and the vast earthwork of Durrington Walls show where people may have lived and feasted while the monument was being used. A little further south, Old Sarum's ancient hilltop and Salisbury Cathedral, with one of the original copies of Magna Carta, make it easy to spend a whole weekend exploring this corner of Wiltshire.
